overclaims: Anthropic's August 2025 threat report describes a criminal who used Claude Code to extort at least 17 organizations, and AI-built ransomware sold to other criminals.
Read plainly, this is a lot of GenAI-driven cybercrime within the first year after the post.
checks.note: Anthropic reports at least 17 organizations targeted, not 17 confirmed extortion victims. Full-year 2025 FBI totals extend beyond the first anniversary of the December 12, 2024 post; they cannot establish that those totals occurred within its first year.

overclaims: Risk is about how likely future harm is, so observed events cannot settle it either way.
Reviewers could reasonably treat the claim as near-self-evident and score it supported on the basis of documented agentic misuse.
This assessment does not, because no measure exists.
checks.note: The contract says a single observed outcome cannot settle the claim; it permits controlled comparisons. The rationale broadens that to observed events generally. Calling support near-self-evident is unsupported editorializing. No specified measure or qualifying study does not establish that no measure exists.

overclaims: The Mintz NDAA note was published a week after the post, but it describes the state of affairs at the post date.
Even the one AI-related law did not regulate AI generally.
checks.note: Mintz describes congressional passage on December 18, after the December 12 post. Its description of the provisions as the first supports an inference about the earlier date, but the payload should distinguish those periods. The evidence explanation also calls the bill a law although the cited report says presidential signature was still expected.

overclaims: Data showing AI-related crime rising after 2024 cannot be credited to the delay rather than to wider AI use.
Cross-jurisdiction comparisons (for example EU versus US) would be confounded by many other differences.
checks.note: No admitted evidence establishes a post-2024 increase in AI-related crime or examines wider AI use as an alternative explanation. Frame this as a hypothetical causal limitation. Cross-jurisdiction confounding is a methodological risk, not an established inevitable result; the contract expressly allows credible controlled comparisons.
